Diagnosis in TCM rests on four methods (Si Zhen), used together. Inspection (Wang) looks at the general appearance, facial color, state of the spirit, posture and above all the tongue: color, shape, coating. Auscultation and olfaction (Wen) means listening to the voice, breathing and cough, as well as noting odors. Inquiry (Wen, with a different tone in Chinese) is a detailed interview: pain, cold or heat, sweating, appetite, sleep, stool, urine, menstrual cycle, emotions. Palpation (Qie) includes taking the pulse at the wrist and palpating painful areas or points.

From China, the practice traveled east. Via Buddhist and diplomatic routes it reached Korea and Japan in the first centuries AD, and there it acquired its own forms, for example the Japanese style, gentler, with very thin needles. In Europe, information arrived through Jesuit missionaries in the 17th century, and the Dutch physician Willem ten Rhijne wrote about acupuncture in 1683. In the 20th century, the French diplomat Georges Soulié de Morant popularized it in France. Western interest grew greatly after 1971–1972, when the American president’s visit to China and a press report about a surgical operation drew public attention.
